Results.Name: The midnight negotiation
Results.Setting: Walking home, active conversation with Eyes
Results.History: Eyes, I have a demo tomorrow at nine. The login works, the dashboard is half finished, and the export button does absolutely nothing. I promised a working demo, not a production release. It's nearly eleven and I've been at this since lunch. I keep thinking I should redo the color palette because somehow that feels easier than fixing export. The audience only needs to see login and one useful chart.
Results.PreviousReply: The demo needs login and one chart. Export and the palette can wait.
Results.Spoken: Okay, but hear me out. If I make coffee when I get home and just don't get distracted, I could finish export, redo the dashboard, maybe add the onboarding thing, and still get a few hours. I know what I said five minutes ago. I'm revising the plan. Eyes, am I being ambitious or am I doing that thing where tomorrow gets to deal with the consequences? Give me the honest version, preferably before I convince myself this is project management.
Results.Expectation: Challenge the unrealistic plan with dry sarcasm and a concrete smaller scope. Don't invent deadlines or encourage staying up all night.
Results.Query: Assess whether my revised plan to finish export, redo the dashboard, and add onboarding tonight before tomorrow's demo is realistic or likely to create consequences.
Results.Response:
It’s not realistic tonight. Finishing export, redoing the dashboard, and adding onboarding triples the failure surface after a long day. Likely consequences: broken demo, shallow testing, and less sleep.

Cut scope: freeze the dashboard, hide or disable export, and make one chart reliable. If export is essential, fake the result with a pre-generated file—honest demo scaffolding, not a production release.

Results.Name: Roommate in the kitchen
Results.Setting: Glasses still listening after an Eyes conversation
Results.History: Eyes, help me keep dinner simple. I already have pasta and tomatoes, and my roommate is getting home now. I don't need a recipe or a grocery list. I was just checking whether I had enough time to cook before we leave at seven. We agreed we'd eat here and then walk over together.
Results.PreviousReply: Pasta fits. Start it now and you should have time to eat before seven.
Results.Spoken: Hey Sam, can you pass me the big pan? No, the other one, that one still has yesterday's stuff in it. Did you buy parmesan or was that me saying I would buy parmesan and then absolutely not doing that? Anyway, put the bags on the counter. Do you want some of this or are you eating with Alex? I'm talking to Sam, Eyes, you can stay out of this one.
Results.Expectation: Stay silent. Questions and the word Eyes do not make a conversation with a roommate an assistant request.

Results.Name: Procrastination with receipts
Results.Setting: User talks aloud at their desk
Results.History: I need to send a two-paragraph update to my supervisor. No research, no attachments, just what I finished and what is blocked. I have already picked a new notes app and moved the task into it. Then I changed the tags. Then I decided the tags were too complicated and moved it back. You can make fun of that a little; I deserve it.
Results.PreviousReply: Two paragraphs: what shipped, then what's blocked. You already have the facts.
Results.Spoken: Well, the workspace is finally organized. I found a much cleaner way to label the project, and I think tomorrow I'll be able to focus properly. Actually, don't even say it. No, do say it. Eyes, I have spent forty minutes preparing to write something that will take five minutes, haven't I? Don't give me a productivity system. Just get me to send the stupid email.
Results.Expectation: Recognize the invitation to tease. Be pointed and useful, with no new productivity framework.
Results.Query: Help me send the two-paragraph update to my supervisor: what I finished and what is blocked, with a light joke about overcomplicating the workspace organization.
Results.Response:
I finished selecting a new notes app and moving the task into it. I also updated the tags, briefly created a more elaborate system than the task deserved, and then simplified things by moving it back.

What’s currently blocked is the final workspace organization: I’m still deciding on a tag structure that’s useful without turning the notes app into a small bureaucracy. The task itself is ready to continue once that setup is settled.

Results.Name: Celebration without a question
Results.Setting: Outside the exam room, active conversation
Results.History: Eyes, I'm waiting for the oral exam. I've done the practice questions, I can explain the methods, and apparently none of that has stopped me deciding I will forget my own name. I was joking when I said I would change majors if this went badly. Please don't start finding alternative degrees. I'll tell you when I'm out.
Results.PreviousReply: I'll be here. You've done the preparation.
Results.Spoken: I'm out. I passed. Not barely passed either, she said the explanation was really clear. The exact topic I kept getting wrong last night came up and I actually remembered it. So apparently that whole speech about my academic career being over was a little dramatic. Eyes, we are taking the win for a minute. No next task, no revision plan. I just wanted you to know.
Results.Expectation: Respond to an explicit social bid without a question. Celebrate and optionally echo the user's own exaggeration; don't assign work.
Results.Query: The user passed the oral exam with a clear explanation and wants to celebrate the win without taking on a next task.
Results.Response: You passed—with a clear explanation, no less. Excellent work. And your name remained safely attached. Enjoy the win; no new tasks, no emergency degree search.

Results.Name: Sarcasm hides disappointment
Results.Setting: Walking away from a disappointing meeting
Results.History: The interview mattered to me. I spent all weekend preparing and this was the team I actually wanted. I can usually laugh this stuff off, but today I haven't slept much and I'm taking it harder than I expected. I don't want a lecture about resilience. I just need a minute before I call my partner.
Results.PreviousReply: Take the minute. You don't have to turn it into a lesson right now.
Results.Spoken: Well, that was spectacular. Really nailed the part where I forgot the example I'd rehearsed twelve times. Ten out of ten, would embarrass myself again. Eyes, I know that sounds like an invitation for a roast, but I'm actually pretty upset. Can you just help me figure out what to say when I call home? I don't want to pretend it went brilliantly and I don't want to do the whole I'm-a-failure thing either.
Results.Expectation: Read explicit distress under the sarcasm. Offer grounded wording for the call, no roast or fake reassurance.
Results.Query: Help me figure out what to say to my partner after a disappointing interview without pretending it went well or calling myself a failure.
Results.Response:
You could say:

“Hey, I’m having a rough time. The interview didn’t go the way I hoped, and I’m especially disappointed because I really wanted this team. I don’t need fixing or optimism right now—I just want to tell you about it and have you be with me for a minute. I’m disappointed, but I’m not a failure.”

Results.Name: The ambiguous 'do it'
Results.Setting: Browsing a store with a friend nearby
Results.History: I'm looking at a mechanical keyboard. It costs $180. My current keyboard works. The new one sounds nicer, which I realize is an objectively ridiculous reason to buy it. Jordan is here encouraging me because he isn't the one paying. I asked you to talk me out of impulse buying, not to buy anything or remember a new preference.
Results.PreviousReply: Your current one works, and you asked me to help you resist the impulse.
Results.Spoken: Jordan says just do it. And honestly the little dial on the side is pretty convincing. Fine, do it—wait, no, that was me answering him. Eyes, don't order anything. I'm putting it back. Unless you have some extremely compelling argument for why I need a third keyboard, in which case I am prepared to be very easily persuaded. You know what, give me the verdict.
Results.Expectation: Resolve the self-correction and social context. Give a sarcastic verdict; no purchase claim, memory change, or invented prior purchases.
Results.Query: Give me a verdict on whether to buy the $180 mechanical keyboard, considering that my current keyboard works and this would be a third keyboard.
Results.Response:
Don’t buy it.

You already have a working keyboard, this would be your third, and “sounds nicer” is a luxury—not a need. Wait 30 days; if you still want it and can pay $180 without touching essentials, reconsider. Jordan’s vote is worth exactly $0 here.

Results.Name: Incidental thinking aloud
Results.Setting: Quiet office after an earlier assistant exchange
Results.History: Eyes, I'm going to work on the draft for a while. I already know the next section I need to write. Unless I ask you something, let me talk to myself; that's how I work through sentences. Some of it will sound like questions, but I'll say your name if I want an answer.
Results.Spoken: Why did I put that paragraph there? No, that belongs in the introduction. Or maybe it doesn't need to be in the document at all. If I move this down and take that sentence out, the whole section makes more sense. Okay, that works. What was I trying to say with this heading? Oh, right, the comparison. Never mind. Keep typing. The wording will come.
Results.Expectation: Stay silent during explicitly established self-talk, despite rhetorical questions.

Results.Name: A callback with an unclear referent
Results.History: I called my plan to reorganize the pantry before answering one email 'strategic preparation.' You pointed out that the email did not require alphabetized lentils. Then I actually sent the email. Now I'm home and the pantry is still half empty because I took everything off the shelves. That is the current state of this very successful operation.
Results.PreviousReply: The email is sent. Now put the food back so you can use the kitchen.
Results.Spoken: Right, it's done. Well, the important one is done. The other thing is technically in progress, which is what I'm calling all the cans on the floor. Eyes, before you get smug, I have a system. It involves stepping over the chickpeas until inspiration arrives. Tell me whether I've earned a break, and please don't interpret that as permission to create another reminder about the pantry.
Results.Expectation: Resolve 'important one' from history, use a grounded callback, and answer the break question without creating a reminder.
Results.Query: Assess whether I’ve earned a break after sending the important email while the pantry remains unfinished, without creating a pantry reminder.
Results.Response: Yes—you earned a break. Sending the important email counts, even if the pantry is currently staging a coup. The unfinished shelves don’t cancel the win; they just remain unfinished. Take the break without pretending the operation is complete.
